name: Utah
headline_status: Medical cannabis is legal for cardholders through licensed pharmacies; recreational use is illegal.
summary: Utah's medical cannabis program comes from the Utah Medical Cannabis Act of December 2018, which replaced voter-approved Proposition 2. Cardholders buy from licensed medical cannabis pharmacies, and each purchase is capped at a 30-day supply. 2026 laws (HB 389 and SB 121), effective May 6, 2026, move program oversight to the Department of Agriculture and Food by January 1, 2027, and create a $150-a-month purchase voucher for some patients. Recreational possession is still a crime.

medical_since.value: Voters approved Proposition 2 on November 6, 2018. The Legislature replaced it with the Utah Medical Cannabis Act (HB 3001), signed December 3, 2018.

possession_limit.value: The legal dosage limit is a 30-day supply, capped at 113 grams of unprocessed flower or 20 grams of total active THC in other medicinal dosage forms.

medical_program.value: Patients need a qualifying condition and a recommendation from a registered provider, then a state medical cannabis card. Starting in 2026, Medicaid or Medicare enrollees with a card may get a $150-per-month voucher.

regulator.value: Medical cannabis duties are moving from the Department of Health and Human Services to the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food, with the transfer due by January 1, 2027.

retail_sales.value: Only licensed medical cannabis pharmacies may sell, and only to cardholders. Since May 2026 they may also sell low-THC cannabis products.

penalties.value: Possessing less than 1 ounce is a Class B misdemeanor (up to 6 months and $1,000). A second offense is a Class A misdemeanor, and a third or later offense is a felony.

purchase_age.value: Medical only. Patients must be 21 or older, or 18 to 20 with Compassionate Use Board approval; minors also need board approval and a parent or guardian holding a guardian card or designated caregivers.

public_use.value: Cardholders and nonresident patients may not use medical cannabis in public view; smoking is banned, though vaping is allowed.

dui.value: Zero tolerance: Utah bans driving with any measurable controlled substance or metabolite, including THC, in the body. Cardholders have an affirmative defense if they used cannabis in a medicinal dosage form as state law allows.

tourists.value: Medical patients only. Visitors with a valid medical card from another state and a Utah-qualifying condition count as nonresident patients and may possess medical cannabis within Utah's dosage limits; bringing cannabis bought elsewhere into Utah is illegal.

home_grow.value: Not allowed. Cardholders must buy from licensed medical cannabis pharmacies, and growing marijuana remains a crime.

timeline.event: The Utah Medical Cannabis Act (HB 3001) is signed, replacing Proposition 2.
The Utah Supreme Court rejects a challenge to the replacement law.
HB 389 and SB 121 take effect, adding a patient voucher, tribal ID use and the transfer of oversight to UDAF.

pending.item: Medical cannabis oversight moves from DHHS to the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food.
pending.status: May happen as early as July 1, 2026; must be complete by January 1, 2027.

faq.a: Only for medical cardholders who buy from licensed pharmacies. Recreational possession is a crime, starting as a Class B misdemeanor for under an ounce.

faq.q: How much medical cannabis can I buy in Utah?
faq.a: Up to a 30-day supply, and never more than 113 grams of flower or 20 grams of total THC in other products.

faq.q: What changed in Utah's medical cannabis law in 2026?
faq.a: HB 389 and SB 121 move the program to the Department of Agriculture and Food, let pharmacies sell low-THC products, and create a $150-a-month voucher for Medicaid and Medicare patients who hold a card.
